$comment: PURPOSE AND SHAPE: One note per element in a NIST CPRT export of CSF 2.0 (the JSON record list at $.response.elements.elements[*] — 906 elements in the 2.0.0 export). Flat: functions (6), categories (34), subcategories (185), implementation examples (363), withdrawal reasons (91), parties (2) and sort keys (225) all land at one level, discriminated by the level property. PROPERTIES: title (the element's short name where it has one), csf_id (the identity), and level (element_type, the discriminator that tells the six shapes apart once they share a folder). curie is emitted automatically from source.ontology plus the identifier and is deliberately not declared here. BODY: the element's text field as a single '## Description' section. PROPERTIES-VS-BODY RATIONALE: text was previously a frontmatter 'description' value, and it is the only prose this source carries — 23 to 212 characters for a subcategory, up to 271 for a category, up to 278 for an implementation example. Moving it into the body is the point of this revision: a full sentence in YAML is truncated in Obsidian's property panel, awkward to escape, and invisible to body search, whereas identity and the short level discriminator are exactly what Bases tabulates and what the Tier 2 projection indexes, so they stay in frontmatter. The heading is the literal 'Description' because the schema does not admit templated headings (spec/recipe.schema.json, body_entry.heading) and one recipe emits seven element types; 'Description' is the honest generic for all of them. No H1 is emitted: Obsidian already renders the note title, so a heading repeating the identifier or the title is noise. omit_if_empty (the default) keeps the section off the 225 'sort' elements and the 12 categories whose text is empty. Note that CPRT leaves title empty on every subcategory and every withdrawal reason (the outcome statement is in text, not title), so those notes carry an empty title property; that is the source's shape, not a projection choice. RIGHTS: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 is a public-domain United States Government work and the CPRT export can be re-downloaded from https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cprt. Recipe, sample output, and screenshots of generated content may all be committed. Corpus provenance and rights posture: https://cybersader.github.io/crosswalker/reference/framework-corpus/. KNOWN GAP 1 — implementation examples cannot be attached to the subcategory they belong to. CPRT ships them as separate elements plus a SIBLING array, $.response.elements.relationships[*] (1,566 edges across four predicates: projection, external_reference, incorporated_into, moved_to). One iterator yields exactly one row array (src/import/parsers/json-source-core.ts), and the recipe grammar has no join, so each example becomes its own standalone note instead of a section under its subcategory. The workbook-sourced nist-csf-2-flat recipe can carry the examples only because that source denormalizes them into a cell on the subcategory row. KNOWN GAP 2 — the export's external_reference edges (408 of them) are the same cross-framework mapping content as the workbook's Informative References column. Nothing here emits them, deliberately: they are mapping assertions between two ontologies and belong in a crosswalk / mapping-set import (see recipes/import/crosswalks), not flattened onto the concept note, and the grammar has no per-item split-and-map that could turn them into clean links or CURIEs anyway. KNOWN GAP 3 (pre-existing, not introduced here) — the grammar has no row predicate (spec/recipe.schema.json declares no filter/where/only_if key at any level; source.levels names layout levels, it does not select rows), so the 225 'sort' ordering keys and the 2 'party' elements become notes too. Filtering them out is a wizard-side or pre-filter concern.
